engine_rules.name: Follow 4-step sequence for every chord melody arrangement
engine_rules.falsifier: Skipping any of the four steps when beginning a new arrangement
engine_rules.anchor: Pick a suitable tune • Change the key if necessary for better range and playability • Learn the melody on top 2 (or 3) strings • Choose chord voicings to add below melody notes

_provenance.section_title: How to Arrange Chord Melodies — The Basic in a Nutshell

engine_rules.name: Choose a ballad for a first chord melody arrangement
engine_rules.falsifier: Choosing a fast bebop tune for a first chord melody project
engine_rules.anchor: I recommend you stick to ballads, rather than the faster bebop tunes

engine_rules.name: Prioritize tunes with long-held melody notes for first arrangements
engine_rules.falsifier: Selecting a tune with predominantly short, fast melody notes for a beginner arrangement
engine_rules.anchor: The slower tempo and longer-held melody notes in ballads will be much easier for your first project.

engine_rules.name: Choose a key that places the melody on the top 3 strings between the 3rd and 9th fret
engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement where melody consistently falls above the 12th fret or below the 3rd fret on the top strings
engine_rules.anchor: Search for a key where you can play the melody on the top 3 strings, roughly anywhere from the 3rd to the 9th fret.

_provenance.section_title: Step 2 — Change Key if Necessary for Range and Playability

engine_rules.name: Avoid keys where arrangement sits too high — causes lack of depth
engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement with melody on top strings but above 12th fret sounding balanced
engine_rules.anchor: If the arrangement is too high, it will sound like it doesn't have enough depth.

_provenance.section_title: Step 2 — Change Key if Necessary for Range and Playability

engine_rules.name: Avoid keys where arrangement sits too low — causes muddy, dark sound
engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement with melody on lower strings below 3rd fret sounding clear and balanced
engine_rules.anchor: if your arrangement is too low in the register, it will sound too dark and muddy.

_provenance.section_title: Step 2 — Change Key if Necessary for Range and Playability

engine_rules.name: Experiment with multiple keys to find correct register
engine_rules.falsifier: Committing to original key without testing register suitability
engine_rules.anchor: Finding the ideal range is usually what will dictate your choice of key. You'll need to experiment to find a key that works.

_provenance.section_title: Step 2 — Change Key if Necessary for Range and Playability

engine_rules.name: Transpose Autumn Leaves from Gm to Em for better chord melody register
engine_rules.falsifier: Autumn Leaves in Gm with melody confined to top 3 strings between 3rd and 9th fret
engine_rules.anchor: Some of those notes of Autumn Leaves in Gm are too low

_provenance.section_title: Step 2 — Change Key if Necessary for Range and Playability

engine_rules.name: Place melody primarily on strings 1 and 2, occasionally string 3
engine_rules.falsifier: Melody confined to strings 4–6 preventing chord voicings underneath
engine_rules.anchor: We need to be able to play the melody on the top 2 strings (maybe dipping into the 3rd string occasionally)

_provenance.section_title: Step 3 — Learn the Melody on the Top 2 (or 3) Strings

engine_rules.name: Play melody horizontally across the fretboard rather than staying in one position
engine_rules.falsifier: Melody stays in a single positional box on the top strings
engine_rules.anchor: you will need to play more horizontally over the fretboard, rather than staying in a single position

_provenance.section_title: Step 3 — Learn the Melody on the Top 2 (or 3) Strings

engine_rules.name: Adapt melody fingering to top-string position even if it changes original shape
engine_rules.anchor: notice how the fingering has been adapted with this in mind

_provenance.section_title: Step 3 — Learn the Melody on the Top 2 (or 3) Strings

engine_rules.name: Place chord voicings on strings below the melody strings
engine_rules.falsifier: Chord voicings placed on strings 1 or 2 competing with the melody
engine_rules.anchor: With the melody notes fingered on the high strings, we can now place chord voicings underneath the melody notes.

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Do not place a chord on every melody note
engine_rules.falsifier: Every single melody note harmonized with a chord voicing causing clutter
engine_rules.anchor: You don't need a chord on every melody note.

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Place chords primarily on long-held melody notes
engine_rules.falsifier: Avoiding chords on long-held notes while harmonizing short passing tones
engine_rules.anchor: I mainly place chords on the long-held melody notes. It sounds great and is easy on the hands.

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Too many chords makes arrangement cluttered and difficult
engine_rules.anchor: Too many chords can make your arrangement sound cluttered and make it difficult to play.

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Use chord voicing to emphasize chord change instead of sustaining long melody notes
engine_rules.falsifier: Avoiding chord placement at chord change points
engine_rules.anchor: rather than trying to hold them for their full length, I place a chord voicing to emphasize the change of chord instead.

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Adapt melody durations to account for guitar note decay
engine_rules.falsifier: Writing melody as if guitar can sustain notes for their full written duration
engine_rules.anchor: The long melody notes ring out quickly on guitar, so rather than trying to hold them for their full length

_provenance.section_title: Step 4 — Choose Chord Voicings to Add Below Melody Notes

engine_rules.name: Choose one right-hand technique and commit to it for the course
engine_rules.anchor: think about which approach you would like to use for this course and what you are familiar with technique-wise already

engine_rules.name: Use fingerstyle to create intricate arpeggio figures and independent voice movement
engine_rules.falsifier: Fingerstyle producing only block chords without independent voice movement
engine_rules.anchor: Notice the intricate arpeggio figures I can create with this technique.

engine_rules.name: Use thumb (or thumbpick) for bass notes in fingerstyle chord melody
engine_rules.falsifier: Using fingers rather than thumb for bass string articulation in fingerstyle
engine_rules.anchor: To pluck the bass notes, you can use your thumb by itself

engine_rules.name: Consider thumbpick for executing single-line passages within fingerstyle chord melody
engine_rules.anchor: consider Lenny Breau's approach of using a thumb pick. This can be helpful to play single lines easily like a plectrum player when you need it.

engine_rules.name: Use block chords (strum) as primary voicing approach for plectrum chord melody
engine_rules.falsifier: Attempting intricate polyphonic arpeggio figures with plectrum only
engine_rules.anchor: your options may be more limited as you need to find voicings where you can strum the chord mostly as block chords rather than the more intricate polyphony of fingerstyle

engine_rules.name: Recognize that block chord strumming with plectrum adds drive and swing not available with fingerstyle
engine_rules.anchor: strumming block chords in this way can give the arrangement more drive and swing

engine_rules.name: With plectrum, pluck bass note first then quickly strum remaining chord strings
engine_rules.falsifier: Strumming all strings simultaneously from bass to treble with plectrum
engine_rules.anchor: pluck the bass note first, followed by a quick strum of the rest of the chord

engine_rules.name: Do not use hybrid picking as primary technique for chord melody
engine_rules.anchor: for chord melody, we usually recommend using either fingerstyle or using a regular plectrum.

engine_rules.name: Note that hybrid picking is ergonomically awkward due to pinky finger length
engine_rules.anchor: Personally, I find this technique awkward especially due to the shorter length of the pinky finger.

engine_rules.name: Adapt course examples from fingerstyle to plectrum block chords if desired — both are valid
engine_rules.anchor: Most of the examples in the course will be fingerstyle, but you can easily tweak the examples to use block chords suitable for the strumming plectrum style.

engine_rules.name: Cover All Scale Degrees With Voicings

then.voicing.collection: one voicing per scale degree of the target key
then.voicing.density: full chord under each melody note

engine_rules.falsifier: A scale degree exists with no assigned voicing in the collection
engine_rules.anchor: You'll be able to harmonize any melody note that's on a chord from the G Major chord family

_provenance.section_title: Step 1–4: Building the First Major Chord Collection (G Major)

engine_rules.name: Transpose Collection by Shifting Shapes to New Root

when.target.key: any key other than the collection's original key

then.voicing.shape: identical shapes shifted to start on the new root fret
then.voicing.fret_offset: distance from original root fret to new root fret

engine_rules.falsifier: Shapes change form rather than merely shifting position when moving to the new key
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how the shapes are exactly the same as G Major, I've just shifted them up to start on the 8th fret instead of the third fret.

_provenance.section_title: Step 5: Transpose the Chord Collection to Other Keys

engine_rules.name: Drop Shapes Down an Octave When Position Becomes Too High
engine_rules.falsifier: Shape stays at high position and remains playable without strain
engine_rules.anchor: So, let's drop some shapes down the octave when they start to get a bit too high. This is a much more practical way to practice the chord shapes for this key.

_provenance.section_title: Step 5: Transpose the Chord Collection to Other Keys

engine_rules.name: Add Color Notes With Free Fingers to Basic Chord Voicings

then.voicing.tensions: add available extensions with unused fingers on adjacent strings

engine_rules.falsifier: All fingers are already assigned in the base voicing with no free fingers available
engine_rules.anchor: Experiment with adding extra notes with your free fingers to the chord voicings for more interest.

engine_rules.name: Intersperse Single-Line Runs Between Chord Voicings

then.voicing.density: alternate between full chord voicings and single-note lines

engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement consists exclusively of unbroken chord voicings with no linear passages
engine_rules.anchor: You can also play some single lines in between the chord voicings to mix things up.

engine_rules.name: Shapes Within a Collection Are Order-Independent

then.voicing.collection: any shape from the key's collection in any order

engine_rules.falsifier: A specific ordering is required for harmonic coherence with the backing
engine_rules.anchor: any of the shapes in any order will generally sound fine.

engine_rules.name: Chord Vocabulary Must Cover All Three Harmonic Families

then.voicing.collection: includes major voicings, minor voicings, and dominant voicings

engine_rules.falsifier: Collection lacks any one of: major voicings, minor voicings, dominant voicings
engine_rules.anchor: we also need minor and dominant chords in addition to major chords if we are going to be able to make chord melody arrangements.

then.voicing.collection: ii chord = minor voicing, V chord = dominant voicing, I chord = major voicing
then.voicing.quality: one from each harmonic family per progression

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicings for the three families are learned in isolation with no ii-V-I context
engine_rules.anchor: The ii-V-I progression contains a chord from each harmonic family: ii — minor, V - dominant, I - major

then.voicing.collection: Dm7b5 chord collection

then.voicing.collection: m7b5 at ii position, 7alt at V position, minor chord at i position

engine_rules.falsifier: m7b5 and 7alt learned in isolation without progression context

then.voicing.collection: reference library for lookup during arrangement; not required to be memorized upfront

engine_rules.name: Read Chord Symbol as an Interval Formula

then.voicing.quality: derived from the interval formula encoded in the symbol (e.g., Maj7 = 1-3-5-7)

engine_rules.falsifier: Chord voicing contradicts the interval formula of its symbol
engine_rules.anchor: Each symbol you see stands for a formula of intervals: For example: Maj7 formula = 1357 So Cmaj7 =CEGB

engine_rules.name: Construct Chords by Stacking Diatonic Thirds on the Root

then.voicing.quality: built by adding thirds: root → 3rd → 5th = triad; add 7th = jazz chord

engine_rules.falsifier: Chord notes are not a stack of consecutive thirds from the root
engine_rules.anchor: Chords are constructed most often by stacking thirds.

engine_rules.name: Three Notes Is the Minimum for a Chord
engine_rules.falsifier: Two-note dyad presented as a full chord
engine_rules.anchor: A triad is the smallest amount of notes you can have for a chord.

engine_rules.name: Adding a Fourth Third to a Triad Creates a Jazz 7th Chord
engine_rules.falsifier: Fourth stacked third does not produce a 7th-chord quality
engine_rules.anchor: We can continue to stack an extra third on top of these triads, giving us 4 note chords or 'jazz' chords - aptly named because of the jazzy sound this extra 3rd gives us

engine_rules.name: Label Scale Degrees 2, 4, 6 as 9, 11, 13 When Used as Chord Extensions
engine_rules.falsifier: Extension above the 7th labeled as 2, 4, or 6 in a chord symbol
engine_rules.anchor: as we continue through the series of 3rds, we get into numbers like 9,11, and 13. This is where chords like GMaji3 come from

_provenance.section_title: Understanding Numbers in Chord Symbols — Extensions: 9, 11, 13

engine_rules.name: Chords Containing 9, 11, or 13 Are Called Second-Octave Structures
engine_rules.anchor: chords that include the 9th, 11th, or 13th are often called 'second octave structures'.

_provenance.section_title: Understanding Numbers in Chord Symbols — Extensions: 9, 11, 13

engine_rules.name: Omit the 5th to Simplify Voicings Without Losing Harmonic Essence

when.harmonic.context: complex chord with too many notes to play

engine_rules.falsifier: Removing the 5th changes the essential harmonic quality of the chord
engine_rules.anchor: Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th.

engine_rules.name: Omit the Root When Necessary for Playability

then.voicing.density: remove root from guitar voicing (bass player covers it)

engine_rules.falsifier: Chord loses harmonic identity when root is removed and no bass instrument covers it
engine_rules.anchor: Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th.

engine_rules.name: Omit the 11th in Complex Voicings When Needed
engine_rules.anchor: Intervals most commonly omitted include the 5th, the root (1st), the 11th, and the 9th.

engine_rules.name: Even the 3rd and 7th May Be Omitted in Very Complex Chords
engine_rules.falsifier: Chord retains clear harmonic identity without 3rd or 7th
engine_rules.anchor: even the 3rd and the 7th can be omitted for more complex chords in certain situations as well.

engine_rules.name: Distinguish the Theoretically Correct Chord From the Playable Guitar Voicing

then.voicing.density: omit non-essential notes to achieve playability while preserving chord essence

engine_rules.falsifier: Guitar voicing contains every theoretical note of the chord with no playability issues
engine_rules.anchor: On the guitar, there is a difference between the theoretically correct chord and the playable chord.

engine_rules.name: Write Diatonic Extensions Without Parentheses in Chord Symbol

when.voicing.tensions: interval naturally occurs in the parent key scale

then.voicing.quality: extension written as part of the chord name (e.g., G9, G13, GMaj9)

engine_rules.falsifier: Diatonic extension enclosed in parentheses in the chord symbol
engine_rules.anchor: An extension (sometimes called a 'natural' or 'diatonic' tension) is an interval of the chord which naturally occurs in the parent scale of the key of the progression. Extensions are included as part of the chord name.

engine_rules.name: Write Altered Tensions in Parentheses After the Chord Name

when.voicing.tensions: interval outside the parent key scale

then.voicing.quality: altered tension written in parentheses after the chord name (e.g., G7(b13#9))

engine_rules.falsifier: Altered tension written without parentheses as if it were a diatonic extension
engine_rules.anchor: Altered tensions are notes that are outside the parent scale of the key of the progression, and are (usually) added in parentheses after the chord name.

engine_rules.name: Read Slash Chord as Target Chord Over Specified Bass Note

then.voicing.quality: play chord X with Y as the lowest sounding note
then.voicing.strings: lowest string carries the bass note Y

engine_rules.falsifier: Chord played without the indicated bass note as the lowest pitch
engine_rules.anchor: Slash chords are a way to indicate what note should be in the bass of a chord. For example: G6/E means to play a G6 chord with an E as the lowest note.

engine_rules.name: Prioritize Slash Chord Accuracy in Solo Guitar Arranging

then.voicing.strings: bass note voiced on lowest available string as specified by slash symbol

engine_rules.falsifier: Solo arrangement ignores the slash bass note entirely
engine_rules.anchor: they are useful to know what this means and can give you some interesting possibilities, especially for solo jazz guitar.

engine_rules.name: Choose Chord Name Based on Harmonic Context, Not Note Content Alone

when.harmonic.context: ambiguous chord (same notes could imply multiple symbols)

then.voicing.quality: name that best describes the chord's function in the surrounding progression

engine_rules.falsifier: The same note group always receives the same chord name regardless of progression context
engine_rules.anchor: A chord's sound is as much defined by the chords that are around it in the progression, just as much as the notes of the chord themselves.

engine_rules.name: A Rootless Voicing May Function as a Different Chord in a New Context

when.harmonic.context: voicing placed in a different progression

then.voicing.quality: re-labeled as the chord whose root is implied by the new context (e.g., CMaj7 without root = Am9)

engine_rules.falsifier: Re-labeled chord is not actually spelled by the notes of the voicing in the new context
engine_rules.anchor: it could also be an Am9 chord (with the A root omitted) if you place it in this progression instead

engine_rules.name: Generate New Voicings by Adding, Removing, or Altering Notes on a Known Shape

then.voicing.shape: modified from base by adding/removing/raising/lowering one note at a time
then.voicing.tensions: new extension or alteration introduced by the changed note

engine_rules.falsifier: No new voicing quality emerges from the modification (identical chord quality)
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how I can turn this into a new voicing by simply adding a note

_provenance.section_title: Finding More Interesting Voicings by Adding, Removing, or Altering Notes

engine_rules.name: Track the Interval of the Top Note in Each Voicing for Chord Melody Use

then.voicing.quality: top note interval identified and labeled (e.g., 9, #4, #9, b13, etc.)
then.voicing.string_set: highest string carries the melody note whose interval is catalogued

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing selected for chord melody without knowing which interval of the chord appears on top
engine_rules.anchor: The number below each voicing indicates the interval of the top note of the voicing, which is very useful to know for chord melody arranging as you'll see in future lessons!

_provenance.section_title: Finding More Interesting Voicings by Adding, Removing, or Altering Notes

engine_rules.name: Identify the Chord Name of Each Newly Generated Voicing

when.harmonic.context: newly created voicing from alteration method

then.voicing.quality: chord name derived from the interval content of the new voicing

engine_rules.falsifier: New voicing used without identifying its chord name
engine_rules.anchor: see if you can work out what the chord name would be for the new voicings you have created.

_provenance.section_title: Finding More Interesting Voicings by Adding, Removing, or Altering Notes

engine_rules.name: Label every melody note by its interval relative to the active chord before selecting voicings

then.voicing.collection: defer until interval map complete

engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement where voicings are chosen without prior interval analysis and still achieves consistent chord-tone melody alignment
engine_rules.anchor: Carefully going through the progression in this way, we can label the intervals in the melody in relation to the chords in the progression as follows

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Melodic Interval Analysis — Fly Me to the Moon

engine_rules.name: Assign anticipation melody notes to the upcoming chord, not the current one

when.harmonic.context: melody note arrives one beat before chord change

then.arrangement.add_element: re-label note as interval of next chord

engine_rules.falsifier: Anticipation note that resolves correctly when labelled as interval of the *current* chord rather than the next
engine_rules.anchor: Sometimes a melody note anticipates the next chord so is considered an interval of that chord (see the ends of bar 1, 3, 5, 7).

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Melodic Interval Analysis — Fly Me to the Moon

engine_rules.name: Place chord voicings at the first melody note of each bar or chord change, not on every note

then.arrangement.add_element: chord voicing on downbeat or chord-change beat only

engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement with chord on every melody note that is still rated more playable and musical than one with bar-start placement only
engine_rules.anchor: This final step is a straightforward process of applying a chord to the first melody note of each bar and/or chord change in the lead sheet.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Applying Chords to the Melody — The Chord-Dictionary Method

engine_rules.name: Select voicing via three-key lookup: (1) melody string, (2) chord quality, (3) melody interval

then.voicing.collection: chord dictionary filtered by [melody.string, chord_quality, melody.interval]

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing selected without knowing melody string, chord quality, or interval that nonetheless produces consistent chord-tone melody alignment
engine_rules.anchor: To know which voicing to pick we need to establish: 1. The string the melody note is on 2. The type of chord that is in the chord progression whilst that melody note is played 3. The interval of the melody note in relation to that chord.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Applying Chords to the Melody — The Chord-Dictionary Method

engine_rules.name: The highest note of the chosen voicing must equal the melody note interval (or be adaptable to it)

then.voicing.strings: top note on same string as melody note

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing where inner-voice note equals melody and top note does not, yet melody remains audible and clear
engine_rules.anchor: Choose chord voicings that have the same interval of the melody note as the highest note in the chord shape.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Applying Chords to the Melody — The Chord-Dictionary Method

engine_rules.name: If dictionary voicing key doesn't match, shift the shape along the fretboard until its top note lands on the melody fret

when.harmonic.context: dictionary voicing found in wrong key

then.voicing.shape: same shape, transposed up/down so top note = melody fret

engine_rules.anchor: Easily fixed - just shift the shape down on the fretboard so that the top note matches the same fret where the melody note is on our score

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Applying Chords to the Melody — The Chord-Dictionary Method

engine_rules.name: For a minor chord with b3 melody on string 1, use a minor voicing with b3 as top note on string 1 (e.g. shape 1322 shifted to melody fret)

then.voicing.shape: x x 1 3 2 2 (relative), top note = b3 on string 1

engine_rules.falsifier: Minor voicing with 5th or root as top note on string 1 that produces clearer chord-tone melody than b3-top voicing
engine_rules.anchor: So, we need to pick a chord from our dictionary with a b3 as the note on the top string

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Applying Chords to the Melody — The Chord-Dictionary Method

engine_rules.name: Prefer sparse chord placement over harmonising every melody note

then.voicing.density: reduced — chords at key structural points only

engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement rated superior by musician panel where every melody note carries a chord voicing
engine_rules.anchor: less is more — placing chords at key places 'here and there' is easier on the hands and is usually more than enough to imply the harmony beneath the melody line. So don't get carried away!

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives

engine_rules.name: When a voicing is too difficult, first try removing low or doubled notes to ease the fretting hand

then.voicing.density: reduced by removing lowest or doubled note

engine_rules.falsifier: Removed low note causes harmonic ambiguity that full voicing would not
engine_rules.anchor: Cut out notes from the chord - e.g. we could cut that low B to make it easier to change to the next chord

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives

engine_rules.name: Substitute block chord with diads (3rds or 6ths) when full voicing is unplayable
engine_rules.falsifier: Context where diads produce more hand strain than block chord due to string-skip patterns
engine_rules.anchor: Choose a different harmonization approach - e.g. instead of block chords I could use parallel octaves or diads (a "chord" with only two notes). Here's an example of diads in 3rds

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives

engine_rules.name: Remove a chord voicing entirely when it resists all adaptation — bare melody is preferable to forced awkward voicing
engine_rules.anchor: Removing the difficult voicings completely often makes the whole passage work much better on the guitar — it helps my hands to relax.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives

engine_rules.name: Prioritise ease under the fretting hand — easier fingering is musically better in most contexts

then.voicing.quality: choose most ergonomic realisation of harmonic intent

engine_rules.falsifier: Passage where technically difficult voicing is unanimously judged to sound better than easier alternative in controlled listener study
engine_rules.anchor: If it's easy on the hands, the music will flow better - so most of the time making things as easy as possible is musically the best option anyway

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Making Arrangements Playable — Density, Voicing Cuts, and Alternatives

engine_rules.name: Add at least one extension or alteration to dominant chord voicings to avoid a 'vanilla' jazz sound

then.voicing.tensions: add one alteration or extension (b9, #9, b13, #11, 13 etc.)

engine_rules.falsifier: Dominant chord with no extensions judged more jazz-idiomatic than extended version in a recording context
engine_rules.anchor: The jazzy sound in arrangements usually comes from adding extensions and tensions to voicings - particularly to dominant chords.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Add b13 (Eb) to G7 voicing to produce G7(b13) for characteristic jazz tension

when.harmonic.context: G7 or any V7 in arrangement

engine_rules.falsifier: G7(b13) voicing rated less interesting than plain G7 in blind jazz-guitar arrangement evaluation
engine_rules.anchor: Let's add an Eb to that chord shape to make it a G7(b13) — the Eb is acting as the b13 giving it some cool tension

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: A single added tension note on a dominant chord is sufficient to transform the harmonic colour; do not over-complicate

then.voicing.density: base shell or dictionary voicing + one tension note
then.voicing.tensions: one alteration chosen from b9 / #9 / b13 / #11

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing with three tensions rated clearer and more idiomatic than single-tension version on guitar
engine_rules.anchor: See how just a small touch of tension can make an arrangement sound far more interesting.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: For up-tempo tunes, cut lower-register notes from voicings more aggressively to maintain playability

when.harmonic.context: fast-moving harmonic rhythm or up-tempo melody

then.voicing.density: reduced — lower tones cut, upper chord tones retained

engine_rules.falsifier: Up-tempo arrangement where retaining low bass notes in every voicing is rated more playable than trimmed versions
engine_rules.anchor: Notice how I'm often cutting the lower tones out of the chords to make them more playable for this up-tempo tune.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Complete Arrangements — Fly Me to the Moon and Alone Together

engine_rules.name: Adjust melody rhythm when necessary to make the arrangement lie naturally under the hands

when.harmonic.context: passage where written melody rhythm conflicts with hand coordination

then.arrangement.add_element: rhythmic alteration of melody to suit guitar voicing transitions

engine_rules.anchor: I also had to alter the rhythm of the melody quite a bit to enable the arrangement to be more natural under the hands.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Complete Arrangements — Fly Me to the Moon and Alone Together

engine_rules.name: Use published complete arrangements as learning examples AND as starting points for personal variation

then.arrangement.add_element: learn arrangement verbatim, then adapt personal voicing choices

engine_rules.anchor: You can treat these arrangements as an example to learn on your guitar, or you could use them as a starting point for your own arrangement in the lessons that follow.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Complete Arrangements — Fly Me to the Moon and Alone Together

engine_rules.name: In solo guitar, alternate bass lines, chord blocks, and single-note lines rather than sustaining all simultaneously

then.arrangement.add_element: rotation of bass / chord / single-line textures across measures

engine_rules.falsifier: Solo guitar arrangement sustaining all three layers simultaneously rated more natural than alternating-texture version
engine_rules.anchor: A good solo guitar arranger simply suggests these elements throughout the performance. Play a measure of walking bass, followed by a chord line, followed by unaccompanied single lines — alternating through these different devices gives the 'illusion' to the audience of a complete band.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Use fingerstyle picking for solo guitar voicings requiring simultaneous note sounding
engine_rules.falsifier: Plectrum technique demonstrated to produce cleaner simultaneous voicings than fingerstyle across a range of solo guitar passages
engine_rules.anchor: many of the voicings you are about to learn are quite difficult to play with a pick if you intend to sound the notes simultaneously without tricky muting techniques. For this reason, I gravitate to using fingerstyle picking for solo guitar.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Choose arrangement key (A, E, or D) to exploit open strings as bass notes in solo guitar

then.target.key: prefer A, E, or D for open-string bass availability
then.voicing.strings: use open 5th/6th string bass where available

engine_rules.falsifier: Solo guitar arrangement in Bb or Eb rated more playable than A/E/D arrangement of same piece due to higher-position voicing availability
engine_rules.anchor: Choosing a key like A, E, or D gives you essentially another set of free fingers. Without needing to fret the occasional bass note, you can make things much easier technically.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Ensure bass notes are in a sufficiently low register relative to upper harmony to avoid thin sound

then.voicing.strings: bass note on 5th or 6th string, separated from upper harmony by at least one octave where possible

engine_rules.falsifier: Solo guitar arrangement with bass and melody within one octave rated as full-sounding by listener panel
engine_rules.anchor: A common issue with many jazz guitar arrangements is that the bass is too close to the upper harmony, which results in a thin sound.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Shell voicing = root + 3rd + 7th; omit 5th and all doubled notes
engine_rules.anchor: All we have left is now the root on the bass, the 3rd, and the 7th in these shapes. These are called shell voicings — i.e. the 'bare bones' of what you need to define the sound of the chord: the root, 3rd, and 7th.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Remove the 5th from jazz chord voicings to avoid redundancy and reduce unnecessary fretting

when.arrangement.style: jazz chord melody or solo guitar

engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing including 5th judged clearer or more jazz-idiomatic than 5th-omitted version in blind test
engine_rules.anchor: You can remove the 5th from the chord and still retain the essential character of the sound.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Substitute 6th for 7th in shell voicing to achieve a warmer, more resolved harmonic colour
engine_rules.falsifier: Context where 7th-shell produces a warmer resolved sound than 6th-shell on same chord
engine_rules.anchor: note that the 6th interval can also be used instead of the 7th which gives a warmer, more resolved sound

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: For bass notes on the 6th string, use the root-on-6 shell grid (major, dominant, minor variants)

then.voicing.collection: root-on-6-string shell voicing set

engine_rules.anchor: Root on the 6th String / MAJOR DOMINANT MINOR / CMa7 C6 C7 Cm7

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: For bass notes on the 5th string, use the root-on-5 shell grid; learn both 3rd-on-top and 7th-on-top versions

then.voicing.collection: root-on-5-string shell voicing set, both inversions

engine_rules.anchor: Notice how, for some positions of voicings, you can either have the 3rd as the highest note or the 7th on top instead — it's good to learn both versions.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Always prefer open-string variants of shell voicings over fretted equivalents where available

then.voicing.strings: open string on bass or inner voice

engine_rules.falsifier: Open-string shell voicing that produces unwanted ringing open string causing harmonic clash in a specific progression
engine_rules.anchor: Always look for opportunities to use open strings for these voicings where possible

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Add melody note above shell voicing by selecting the shell-plus-extension shape matching (chord_quality, melody.interval, root.string)

then.voicing.collection: shell-extension grid for matching chord type and root-string

engine_rules.falsifier: Shell-plus-extension voicing where melody note is audibly masked by inner shell voices
engine_rules.anchor: Shell voicings are a convenient way to add a chord underneath melody notes.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: When adding melody note above shell creates a doubled note, cut the doubled inner-voice note
engine_rules.falsifier: Case where doubled note within shell-plus-extension voicing is judged to improve clarity or warmth
engine_rules.anchor: Generally, try to avoid doubling notes in the chord - I've usually cut out notes from the voicing when doubling occurs. However, sometimes it still sounds ok so I've left doublings in when this is the case.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Adapt shell fingering (different fingers, add barre) as needed when incorporating melody note extension

then.voicing.shape: re-finger shell to accommodate extension note

engine_rules.anchor: Sometimes the fingering of the shell voicing needs to be adapted (e.g. different fingers used for the shell voicing or the addition of a barre.)

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

engine_rules.name: Step 1: Verify key contains open-string bass opportunities before arranging

then.target.key: confirm or transpose to key with open-string bass notes
then.arrangement.add_element: note which open strings will serve as bass notes

engine_rules.anchor: The first thing to look at is the key of the progression and register. The second bar has an Am7, which is a good sign — I can use an open A on the 5th string as the bass note in that bar.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Step 2: Shift melody up an octave if it is too low to accommodate chord voicings underneath on the top 2 strings
engine_rules.falsifier: Solo arrangement with melody on strings 3–4 that accommodates full shell voicings below without octave shift
engine_rules.anchor: the melody is too low. Let's shift it up the octave so it's in a better register to fit voicings underneath (also remembering to keep the melody notes mostly on the top 2 strings)

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Step 3: Add a bass note at each chord change before selecting full shell voicings

then.arrangement.add_element: single bass note on 5th or 6th string at each chord change

engine_rules.anchor: To get a feel for where to place shell voicings, a good exercise is to add a bass note underneath the melody at each chord change, like this

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Step 4: Analyse melody intervals relative to chords before applying shell voicings

then.arrangement.add_element: interval label for each melody note against active chord

engine_rules.anchor: Just like we did in the previous module, it's useful to know the interval of the melody notes in relation to the chord progression

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Step 5: Apply shell voicings with bass note at each chord-change position identified in step 3

then.voicing.collection: shell voicing grid (root-on-5 or root-on-6 as appropriate)
then.arrangement.add_element: shell voicing at each bass-note position

engine_rules.anchor: Now it's a straightforward case of adding chord voicings where I have placed each bass note in the progression — let's use those shell voicings we covered in the last lesson

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Step 6 (most important): Refine by cutting notes, swapping voicings, and listening at the instrument until the passage feels and sounds good

then.arrangement.add_element: iterative voicing adjustments: cut notes / swap shapes / adapt fingerings

engine_rules.anchor: Refining an arrangement is the most important step of solo guitar arranging. Making small tweaks, cutting unessential notes, and looking for skillful ways to finger passages to get the arrangement to feel good under the hands and sound good is the aim.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Substitute open string for a fretted bass note when the fretted position causes an awkward stretch

when.harmonic.context: chord with root matching an open string

then.voicing.strings: open 5th or 6th string instead of fretted bass note

engine_rules.anchor: you can change the A bass note to the open 5th string instead

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: When a shell voicing doubles a melody note in an inner voice, swap to an alternative voicing that avoids the doubling

when.harmonic.context: melody descends to a pitch already present in shell

then.voicing.shape: alternative voicing from dictionary that avoids doubling

engine_rules.falsifier: Inner-voice doubling of melody judged to improve warmth or resonance in specific context
engine_rules.anchor: the shell voicing is doubling the 3rd in the melody when that D falls to a C in the melody... This is inefficient and it doesn't sound very good to have that note doubled. So let's resort to an alternative voicing for the D melody note.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Remove doubled root note from voicing when open or fretted bass already provides the root

when.harmonic.context: root appears in both bass string and inner string

engine_rules.falsifier: Arrangement where doubling the root in bass and inner voice produces audibly fuller sound worth the added difficulty
engine_rules.anchor: Doubling the root directly above isn't a big deal and can still sound good, but it is unnecessary. It also makes it a bit awkward to sound 5 notes at once with my plucking hand using fingerstyle. So let's remove the A on the 4th string

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Add a passing or secondary dominant chord to a sparse bar to enrich the harmonic movement

when.harmonic.context: bar sounds harmonically empty or static
when.progression.type: allows chromatic or diatonic passing chord

then.arrangement.add_element: passing chord or V7/V interpolated at appropriate beat
then.voicing.quality: passing dominant or secondary dominant voicing

engine_rules.falsifier: Passing chord that creates hand coordination problem without audible harmonic benefit
engine_rules.anchor: Let's see what happens if you embellish the chord progression and add a V7 chord to the G on the 3rd beat.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Swap repeated chord shapes for alternative voicings to create tonal and textural variety

when.harmonic.context: same chord shape used earlier in same arrangement

then.voicing.shape: alternative voicing from dictionary for same chord/interval
then.voicing.collection: alternate form of previously used shape

engine_rules.falsifier: Repeated identical shapes judged to provide consistent tone preferred over varied shapes in specific arrangement context
engine_rules.anchor: The final chord seems a bit boring to me as it's the same chord shape we used at the start of the arrangement. So let's swap out that shape for another one from our chord dictionary

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Add bass note to a high-register voicing that sounds empty without one

then.arrangement.add_element: bass note on 5th or 6th string added to existing upper voicing

engine_rules.anchor: It sounds a bit empty without a bass note though — let's add a C bass note to that chord voicing

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Treat solo guitar arranging as inherently experimental — start standard, then tweak by listening and hand-feel

then.arrangement.add_element: iterative experimentation — listen, feel hands, adjust

engine_rules.anchor: solo guitar is very much about experimentation and trial and error — starting with a standard approach and then tweaking through a careful process to listening to the sound and noticing what it feels like in the hands.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement
_provenance.section_title: Solo Guitar Arrangement Process — Moon River Case Study

engine_rules.name: Use arpeggiation (sequential note plucking) to add a lyrical, ballad-appropriate texture to chord voicings

then.arrangement.add_element: arpeggio pattern — pluck notes of voicing sequentially rather than simultaneously

engine_rules.falsifier: Arpeggio applied to up-tempo passage that produces rhythmic confusion rather than lyrical effect
engine_rules.anchor: An easy way to get a more impressive sound in your solo guitar arrangements is through arpeggiation. Arpeggiation is when you pluck the notes of a chord one at a time, instead of a block of notes played simultaneously. This can give a more lyrical sound and is especially effective in arrangements of jazz ballads.

_provenance.chapter_title: Complete Chord Melody — Module 3: Creating a Chord Melody Arrangement

then.voicing.density: 2-note octave pair — melody + note one octave below
then.arrangement.add_element: mute intervening string with first finger

engine_rules.name: Octave notes may be strummed for power or individually plucked for precision — experiment for context

when.harmonic.context: melody line needing harmony without full voicing

when.harmonic.context: up-tempo or fast harmonic rhythm passage

engine_rules.anchor: They are particularly useful for faster-moving tunes when you want some padding underneath a melody without it getting too technically tricky.
